q: How do I calculate emissions from Indian coal when my bill shows grade or GCV, not tonnes of standard coal?
title: Indian coal emissions from grade or GCV
short: Convert the coal's calorific value into energy, then multiply by an IPCC CO2 factor per terajoule. Take GCV from the lab report or the grade's band, convert kcal/kg to MJ/kg, reduce GCV to NCV, and apply about 95 t CO2 per TJ. Low-grade Indian coal often comes to 1.3 to 1.7 kg CO2 per kg, well below a generic factor.
audience: Boiler and kiln operators, plant managers

ol: GCV in MJ/kg = GCV in kcal/kg x 4.1868 / 1,000.
NCV = GCV x 0.95. The IPCC notes that for coal NCV is about 5% below GCV; for wet, high-ash coal the gap can be larger, so use a lab NCV if you have one.
Energy in TJ = tonnes of coal x NCV in MJ/kg / 1,000.
CO2 in tonnes = energy in TJ x the IPCC default factor: 94.6 t CO2 per TJ for other bituminous coal, 96.1 for sub-bituminous.

sections.h: Reading the grade on an Indian coal invoice
p: Non-coking coal in India is graded by GCV in bands of 300 kcal/kg, from G1 above 7,000 down to G17 at 2,201 to 2,500. If you only have the grade, use the midpoint of its band and say so. A lab report of the GCV for each consignment is better, because the grade is measured on a standardised basis and the coal you actually burn may be wetter.

sections.h: Why a single factor per kg can mislead
p: A generic factor such as 2.42 kg CO2 per kg is close to what IPCC defaults give for other bituminous coal: 25.8 MJ/kg NCV x 94.6 t CO2 per TJ is about 2.44 kg per kg. Indian non-coking coal is high in ash and much lower in calorific value, so each kilogram holds less carbon. Applying the generic factor to a G11 coal overstates emissions by about half. Imported coal near 6,000 kcal/kg comes out at about 2.26 kg per kg by the same formula, much closer to the generic value.

ul: Purchase invoices or weighbridge slips with tonnes received.
The supplier's or a third-party lab's GCV report for each consignment, with its moisture basis.
Stock at the start and end of the year, so you count coal burned, not coal bought.

example.title: Worked example: 20 tonnes of G11 coal
lines: G11 band 4,001 to 4,300 kcal/kg; midpoint about 4,150 kcal/kg GCV
CO2: 0.330 x 94.6 = 31.2 t CO2, or 1.56 kg CO2 per kg of coal
With a generic 2.42 kg per kg: 20,000 x 2.42 = 48,400 kg, about 48.4 t, 17 t more
example.note: An estimate from the grade midpoint and the IPCC 5% GCV to NCV rule. A lab NCV and the sub-bituminous factor (96.1) would shift it by a few percent.

senseible: Senseible reads tonnes or kilograms from coal invoices and applies a single factor of 2.42 kg CO2 per kg, from IPCC 2006 defaults. It does not read the grade or GCV and adjust the factor, so for low-grade Indian coal its figure will be higher than a GCV-based calculation; keep your own GCV working alongside it.
